cards.explanation: The answer is that he doesn't turn away from them. The text says King Jeroboam “…did not turn away from all the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit.” (2 Kings 14:24) Same name, same road. Two Jeroboams, and this one walks the first Jeroboam's road.

The answer is prophet. The text calls him “…His servant Jonah son of Amittai, the prophet from Gath-hepher.” (2 Kings 14:25) The LORD spoke a word through him, and King Jeroboam's borders came back just as that word said. The word came first, and the borders followed.

The answer is False. Jeroboam “…did evil in the sight of the LORD…” and he didn't turn away from the sins. (2 Kings 14:24) The text says the LORD saw how bitter Israel's affliction was and that there was “…no one to help Israel…” (2 Kings 14:26) So the saving comes from the LORD's care for His people, not from the king's good behavior.

The answer is that He would not blot out Israel's name. The text says the LORD “…had said that He would not blot out the name of Israel from under heaven…” (2 Kings 14:27) And because of that, He saved them by the hand of Jeroboam son of Jehoash. It's a promise on the LORD's side, friends.

The answer is Damascus. The text says Jeroboam “…waged war and recovered both Damascus and Hamath for Israel…” (2 Kings 14:28) That's a big win for a man who still did evil in the LORD's sight. The writer then points to the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Israel for the rest.

The answer is True. The text says Azariah “…did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, just as his father Amaziah had done.” (2 Kings 15:3) His father Amaziah did right too (2 Kings 14:3). Here's a son who follows his dad's good example, and I love to see it, friends.

The answer is sacrificing and burning incense. The text says “the people continued sacrificing and burning incense there.” (2 Kings 15:4) The king did what was right, and the high places were still not taken away. That's the catch in this king's story, bakers.

The answer is leprosy. The text says “…the LORD afflicted the king with leprosy until the day he died, so that he lived in a separate house…” (2 Kings 15:5) That's a hard thing for a king who did what was right, and the text doesn't say why it happened. I think I'll leave that open the way the text does.

The answer is his son Jotham. The text says “…his son Jotham had charge of the palace and governed the people of the land.” (2 Kings 15:5) King Azariah is in a separate house, and his son runs things. When Azariah rests with his fathers, Jotham reigns in his place (2 Kings 15:7).

The answer is that he does just as they did. The text says King Zechariah “…did evil in the sight of the LORD, as his fathers had done.” (2 Kings 15:9) He did not turn away from the sins that Jeroboam son of Nebat had caused Israel to commit. So the text puts him in line with his fathers, friends.

The answer is True. Shallum son of Jabesh “…conspired against Zechariah, struck him down and killed him in front of the people, and reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 15:10) That's a grim way to get a crown. The crown doesn't stay long, as the next verses show.

The answer is four. Right after Zechariah's reign ends, the text says the word of the LORD spoken to Jehu was fulfilled: “Four generations of your sons will sit on the throne of Israel.” (2 Kings 15:12) The LORD said four, and the text says it happened. What the LORD says comes true, friends.

The answer is that they would not open their gates. Menahem attacked Tiphsah and everyone near it “…because they would not open their gates.” (2 Kings 15:16) This is a heavy part of the passage, and I think it hurts to read. I'm going to let it be heavy.
The answer is a thousand talents of silver. The text says “…Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver…” (2 Kings 15:19) Pul is the king of Assyria. That's a LOT of silver to hand over, friends.

The answer is True. The text says Menahem gave the silver “…in order to gain his support and strengthen his own grip on the kingdom.” (2 Kings 15:19) The text states that reason outright. I'd say he wanted that crown held tight.

The answer is wealthy. The text says Menahem “…exacted this money from each of the wealthy men of Israel…” (2 Kings 15:20) Fifty shekels of silver from each man. I'd bet those men did NOT see that coming.

The answer is False. The text says “…the king of Assyria withdrew and did not remain in the land.” (2 Kings 15:20) He takes the silver and goes. I'll say it kindly, friends: that's a very expensive goodbye.

The answer is one of his own officers. The text says “…his officer, Pekah son of Remaliah, conspired against him…” (2 Kings 15:25) Argob, Arieh and fifty men of Gilead are with him. The man who turns on King Pekahiah is his own officer, bakers.

The answer is that he takes them as captives. The text says Tiglath-pileser, king of Assyria, “…took the people as captives to Assyria.” (2 Kings 15:29) He captures places like Gilead, Galilee and all the land of Naphtali first. That's a heavy verse, and I think it hurts.

The answer is True. The text says Hoshea son of Elah “…attacked Pekah, killed him, and reigned in his place.” (2 Kings 15:30) A conspiracy, a king struck down, and a new king in his place. The text says it plainly, friends.

The answer is the Upper Gate of the LORD's house. The text says “Jotham rebuilt the Upper Gate of the house of the LORD.” (2 Kings 15:35) The high places are still standing, but King Jotham does something good at the LORD's house too, bakers.

The answer is Pekah. The text says, “In those days the LORD began to send Rezin king of Aram and Pekah son of Remaliah against Judah.” (2 Kings 15:37) Pekah is the king of Israel from earlier in this passage. So the LORD begins sending Israel's king and Aram's king against Judah.
